Reviewing a calibration: a Steward's guide

pdmS7 documentation

Source: vignettes/steward-guide.Rmd
steward-guide.Rmd

A Custodian calibrates; a Steward decides whether the result is fit to use. The calibration log records every step the Custodian took, but it cannot tell you whether those steps were sound. That is the Steward’s judgement. This guide sets out what to look at, in what order, and what should make you stop.

You need no R to follow it. Everything here is in the report from build_report(), which opens in a browser, or on the Report tab of calibration_app(). Logging a manual calibration shows how a project is built; Inside the logs explains the files.

Your role

Role Does
Owner Accountable for the model’s use. Named in the project; takes no action in the log.
Steward Reviews and signs off, or sends it back. May not sign off work they took part in.
Delegated Steward As Steward, under a recorded delegation.
Custodian Builds the calibration: data, structure, trials, candidate, validation.

The package refuses a sign-off from anyone who wrote a trial, calibration, candidate or validation in the project, checking both the declared name and the computer login.

Reading the report, in order

The report follows the order of the work. Review it in the same order: an error early on invalidates everything after it.

1. Integrity

The first section says whether the record is intact: every entry’s checksum chain, every data file against the checksum taken when it was registered, and every saved series.

  • Green: the record is as written. Carry on.
  • Red: stop. Something was edited after the event, or a data file has changed. Ask the Custodian why before reading further.

For a stronger check, run verify_project(project, rerun = TRUE), or ask the Custodian to. It repeats every model run and confirms each reproduces its recorded output. A mismatch names what changed in the software since the run.

2. Data

The Data section summarises each registered series: rows, period, step, missing values and the longest gap. Check:

  • The periods. Calibration, validation and, if registered, test windows are separate, in that order, and long enough: a few years of calibration at least, and a validation period that includes floods.
  • Missing flow. More than about 10 per cent missing in a window weakens its scores. A long gap in the middle of the only big flood is worse than many short ones.
  • Where the data came from. The source paths and checksums tie the calibration to a specific extract. For data from reach.io, the Hydrometric Data Register gives its provenance.
  • Warning thresholds. If thresholds are registered, are they the current ones, in the right units, and is the rating used for level thresholds the current rating?

Preparing your data lists the checks the Custodian should have run.

3. Structure

Is the model structure reasonable for the catchment, and is the reasoning recorded? If a structure comparison was run, the report ranks the structures on the validation window: a structure chosen despite ranking low needs a stated reason.

4. Calibration path

The path shows every trial and automatic calibration, linked to the run it started from, with the headline score of each. Look for:

  • A path that explains the candidate. You should be able to follow how the Custodian got from the starting structure to the candidate. A candidate that appears from nowhere, or a long run of unexplained trials, needs questioning.
  • Reasoning. Each trial records why it was tried and what the Custodian concluded. Thin reasoning is not a failure in itself, but it makes the calibration harder to defend later.
  • Parameters on a bound. An automatic calibration that ends with a parameter at the edge of its range was stopped by the fence, not by the data. The calibrated value may be fine; it may equally be compensating for a data problem.
  • Starts that disagree. If the automatic starts end at very different parameters with similar scores, the data do not pin those parameters down. The model may still forecast well, but its parameter values should not be read as catchment properties.
  • Stages. In a staged calibration, check that the first stage got the water balance right (volume error close to zero) before the fast stores were fitted.

5. Candidate and validation

This is the heart of the review. The report shows calibration and validation scores side by side, with hydrographs and flow-duration curves for each window.

Sign Suggests
Validation NSE well below calibration NSE (a drop of more than about 0.1) Over-fitting, or a change in the catchment or the gauge between periods
Volume error over about 10 per cent in either window A water-balance problem: rain, PET, area or rating
Good overall scores, poor high-flow signature (fdc_high) The model misses the floods that matter for warnings
Systematically late or early peaks on the hydrograph Surface store time constants, or a time-stamp error in the data
Poor low-flow signature (fdc_low) only Matters for drought work, less for flood forecasting
Threshold CSI low, or many false alarms Not fit for a warning service at that threshold, whatever the NSE

Judge the scores against the purpose. An NSE of 0.75 may be perfectly adequate for a slow chalk river used for drought planning and inadequate for a flashy catchment with a warning service. Look at the hydrographs: a single number hides where the errors are.

6. The test window and the held-back years

If a test window was registered, it is scored once, after every choice is made, and sign-off requires it. A poor test result does not block sign-off, but it must be explained. A test result much worse than validation suggests the validation window was used, perhaps without intending it, to make choices.

Most projects also hold back the two wettest water years, and the test scores them too. Look past the scores, which ordinary days dominate, to the table of peaks:

  • The candidate’s peak against the observed peak. A large miss on floods the model never saw means the calibration does not extrapolate.
  • The range across equally good fits. A wide range means the record cannot pin down the parameters that control large floods, and the candidate’s peak is partly luck.
  • The rating flag. A peak above the highest gauged flow is itself uncertain. Ask whether a miss is the model’s or the rating’s.

If the Data section shows that the calibration window contains many flows above the highest gauging, ask why. Larger floods: extrapolation and the rating explains the table.

Signing off

The sign-off asks you to confirm four things. Only tick each one if you did it:

Item You confirm
integrity The integrity section is clean, or every failure is explained
data The data are the right data, adequately complete, with the right periods
calibration_path The path explains the candidate and the reasoning is adequate
validation The validation (and test) results are fit for the stated purpose

Then write a statement in your own words: what the calibration is fit for, and any limits on its use. “Accepted for flood forecasting; peaks above 50 m3/s are underestimated by about 10 per cent, so treat forecasts above that with caution” is far more useful to the next reader than “Approved.”

sign_off_project(project, statement = "Accepted for flood forecasting; ...",
                 checklist = c(integrity = TRUE, data = TRUE, calibration_path = TRUE,
                               validation = TRUE))

Once signed off, the project accepts no more entries. Runs with exactly the signed-off configuration are then marked as approved in the run log.

Sending it back

If the calibration is not fit for use, do not sign it off. Write a note in the log saying what must change, so the reason is part of the record:

log_note(project, "Not signed off: validation volume error is 18 per cent. Check the rating
change in 2019 before recalibrating.")

If a signed-off calibration later turns out to be wrong, reopen it with reopen_project() and a reason. The original sign-off stays in the record; a later sign-off supersedes it.

A short checklist

  1. Integrity green, or every failure explained.
  2. Periods separate and sensible; missing data acceptable; thresholds current.
  3. Structure reasoned; any comparison supports the choice.
  4. The path explains the candidate; no unexplained parameters on bounds.
  5. Validation close to calibration; volume error small; hydrographs credible; thresholds adequate for warning use.
  6. Test window scored, and any shortfall explained.
  7. A statement that says what the model is fit for, and what it is not.
